headline: Cylinders can cover a regular tetrahedron for less than half its smallest shadow.
scope: The half-area result is for regular tetrahedra; the directionwise result extends to every tetrahedron.
plain: A cylinder cover wraps a solid in straight tubes, and its cost is the total area of the tubes' cross-sections. A classic two-tube cover of a regular tetrahedron costs exactly half the area of its smallest shadow. People asked whether any cover of a convex solid could ever cost less than that. This paper proves that one can, by splitting the two tubes into many slightly tilted ones (Lean proof listed). It also breaks a stronger 2016 conjecture that compares each tube with the shadow in its own direction.
doesNot: This does not find the cheapest possible cover, and the saving it gives is tiny.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Thøger Bang, the two-cylinder tetrahedron example (as later attributed)
scorecard.significanceWhy: It answers a covering question traced to 1951 and a 2016 conjecture, in a specialized area of geometry.

explanation:
Take a regular tetrahedron: a solid with four equal triangle faces. Make every edge 2 units long. Shine a distant light on it and look at its shadow. The shadow's size depends on the direction of the light. The smallest shadow has area √2, about 1.414. It appears when the light shines straight along one edge.

Now try to cover the solid with cylinders. Here a cylinder means a flat shape, its base, slid along a straight line forever in both directions. The base is measured at right angles to that line. The cost of a cover is the total area of its bases. There is a classic cheap cover with just two cylinders. Cut the tetrahedron halfway up. Cover the bottom half with a cylinder running along the bottom edge. Its base is a triangle of area √2/4, about 0.354. Cover the top half the same way, along the top edge. The two bases total √2/2, about 0.707. That is exactly half of the smallest shadow.

The question behind this comes from planks. A plank is the slab between two parallel planes. In 1951, Thøger Bang proved a rule about covering a convex body with planks. A convex body is a solid with no dents or holes. The planks' widths must add up to at least the body's smallest width. For cylinders, the tetrahedron example shows that the same rule with areas fails. Two cylinders cost only half the smallest shadow. Later authors trace this example, and a question, to Bang's 1951 paper. Must every finite cylinder cover cost at least half the smallest shadow? A 2026 survey by William Verreault still lists this as open.

There is also a stronger guess. Divide each base by the body's shadow in that cylinder's own direction, then add the results. In 2016, Károly Bezdek and Muhammad Khan recorded the guess that this sum is always at least one half. In 2009, Bezdek and Alexander Litvak proved it is at least one third. If the stronger guess were true, the half-area rule would follow.

This paper proves that both guesses fail for the regular tetrahedron. It starts from the classic two-cylinder cover. It slices each triangle base into many thin wedges. Each wedge gets its own slightly tilted line. Tilting shrinks the base, because the base is measured across the new line. The one obstacle is gaps. Tilted neighbors can pull apart, and the two halves can separate near the middle.

Two choices close the gaps. Neighboring wedges are tilted so that their shared side lies in one common plane. Each wedge is also stretched a tiny amount past the halfway cut. The stretch costs area, but less than the tilt saves. Measure cost as a share of the smallest shadow, so the classic cover scores 1/2. Write ε for the size of the tilt. The tilt saves about ε²/240, and the stretch costs ε²/500. The net saving is 13ε²/6000, give or take at most 2ε⁴.

Take the largest tilt the theorem allows, ε = 1/2000. The cover then uses 16,000,000 cylinders, each with a triangle base. Adding up all their bases gives about 0.49999999946 of the smallest shadow. The saving is about 5.4 parts in ten billion. It is tiny, but the rule claimed no cover could save anything at all. The cover is always finite, but it needs more cylinders as the tilt shrinks. The result shows that one half is not a floor. It does not say where the true floor lies.

The stronger guess fails for every tetrahedron, not only regular ones. Stretching or squashing space changes each base and its matching shadow by the same factor. So each ratio in the sum stays the same. The plain half-area claim is stated only for regular tetrahedra. Two companion papers build covers below one half by other routes. One uses parallelogram bases instead of triangles. A third gives a general tool for turning smoothly tilting families of segments into finitely many cylinders.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked formal versions of the regular tetrahedron results. Every regular tetrahedron has a finite cover costing strictly less than half its smallest shadow. The stronger ratio sum is also below one half. The companion approximation results are in the same Lean files. The extension to every tetrahedron by stretching is outside the checked statements. No specialists have published a review yet.
hypeCheck: Solid within its area. The saving is about five parts in ten billion. Lean checks the regular tetrahedron statements. The extension to all tetrahedra is outside that check. No specialist review is published.
